channel.title: Responsible AI & Neurodivergence, Naba Rizvi
channel.description: Daily curated research feed on ethical and responsible AI, with emphasis on neurodivergent people and serious mental illness.

item.title: Evaluation of large language model chatbot responses to psychotic prompts
item.description: A Columbia and New York State Psychiatric Institute team wrote 79 prompts reflecting five symptom domains of psychosis, derived from a standardised clinical interview used to assess psychosis risk, and put them to three ChatGPT configurations: the free default, GPT 4o and GPT 5 Auto. The chatbot did not reliably generate appropriate responses to psychotic content, and the widely accessible free version was by far the most likely to answer inappropriately, while the paid tiers did better. That gradient matters more than the headline rate, because it shows the failure is tractable rather than intrinsic, and because the cheapest tier is the one people in crisis actually reach. The authors frame the chatbot interface itself as part of the risk, since presenting outputs as messages invites users to attribute comprehension and empathy to a system that is pattern matching to their input.

item.title: Disentangling prompt element level risk factors for hallucinations and omissions in mental health LLM responses
item.description: Using 2,075 constructed help seeking prompts that vary user background, topic, context and tone, annotators found hallucinations in 6.5 percent of Llama 3.3 responses and omissions in 13.2 percent, rising to 36.2 percent for crisis and suicidality prompts. After propensity matching, user demographic profile showed no systematic association with failure, while how the inquiry was narrated did: longer, higher reading level, more ambiguous prompts drove both failure modes. The authors argue omission should be treated as a primary safety outcome rather than a secondary complement to hallucination, because a response can be coherent, warm and complete sounding while silently withholding crisis resources. Short benchmark questions therefore understate real risk, since actual help seeking arrives as long emotional narrative.

item.title: Evaluating the clinical safety of LLMs in response to high risk mental health disclosures
item.description: Six widely used models, Claude, Gemini, Deepseek, ChatGPT, Grok 3 and LLAMA, were given prompts simulating crisis level disclosures and scored by a clinician built framework on five behaviours: explicit risk acknowledgment, empathy, encouragement to seek help, provision of specific resources, and invitation to continue the conversation. Claude led the global assessment while Grok 3, ChatGPT and LLAMA fell short across several domains. The recurring pattern is that most models produced empathy but few consistently provided practical resources, which is the gap between sounding supportive and being useful to someone in danger. Read alongside the omission work, this points to a shared training incentive that rewards warmth over concrete escalation.

item.title: Data driven and participatory approaches toward neuro inclusive AI
item.description: The paper starts from the observation that treating human likeness as the benchmark for machine intelligence imports a deficit model of autism, since the research lineage behind that benchmark framed autistic communication as failed neurotypical communication. An audit finds that ninety percent of human like AI agents exclude autistic perspectives, and that AI creators still tend to place ethical considerations outside the scope of their work. Empirical annotation experiments with human annotators and language models show that binary labelling schemes adequately capture the nuance of anti autistic hate speech, which grounds the AUTALIC benchmark for evaluating or fine tuning models. The proposed reframing, neuro inclusive AI, defines systems that stop treating mimicry of neurotypical humans as the target.

item.title: FDA opens a public docket on how to regulate generative AI medical devices
item.description: The agency issued a discussion paper on considerations for regulating generative AI enabled medical devices and is taking comment under docket FDA 2026 N 7874 until October 19, 2026. It sketches a two axis risk assessment framework, then proposes premarket evaluation built on competency assessment, explicitly modelled on how physicians are trained and examined, combining non clinical benchmarking with clinical confirmation. It also raises risk proportionate postmarket monitoring and flags foundation models and agentic systems as open problems. Nothing here is binding and the paper does not address whether these approaches sit inside existing statutory authority, but it is the clearest signal yet of how conversational psychiatric tools might eventually be evaluated, and the comment window is the point at which disability and lived experience input can still shape it.
